text: A dark-lantern has a shutter, so its light can be shown or hidden at will. It is carried by someone who wants to see without being seen.
A snake's typical sound is a soft, continuous hiss.
exceptions: Escaping steam or gas makes much the same sound, and not every snake hisses before it acts.

reads: unrepaired breaches gaped in the old park wall
text: The park wall is broken in places, so the grounds are open to anyone. The plan still rests on the shutters Helen was to unfasten.

reads: what seemed to be a hideous and distorted child
text: Something small and writhing darts from the laurels. Watson says it only 'seemed' a child. The household has loose beasts, and I had half expected one on the lawn.
options: A child, perhaps from the gipsies
Something else, or a person in disguise

reads: His hand closed like a vice upon my wrist in his agitation
text: Holmes is startled too. The danger he is guarding against is not the loose animals, since he never planned for them.

reads: That is the baboon
text: The 'child' is the baboon Helen described. It had the run of the grounds, as she said.

reads: slipping off my shoes
text: Shoes off and every word whispered into an ear. The only listener worth fearing is Roylott, through the opening between the rooms. That agrees with the prediction that the watchers would have to sit silent and dark.

reads: The least sound would be fatal to our plans.
text: As predicted, silence is the whole plan. Roylott must go about his night believing the bed holds Helen.

reads: He would see it through the ventilator.
text: Holmes says it outright: a light here would be seen through the ventilator by 'he', plainly Roylott. So the opening leads into his room, as the cigar smell suggested.
If a light here can be seen from his room, Julia's match was seen by Roylott, and he would know she was awake. The whistle after her scream could be his answer to that light.
options: The whistle is Roylott's reaction to seeing the light
The whistle is a fixed signal given whatever happens

reads: I will sit on the side of the bed
text: Holmes puts himself on the bed, where the sleeper's head lies at the end of the rope. He gives Watson the chair and so takes the exposed place himself.

reads: your very life may depend upon it
text: The danger is silent and quick. A man who dozes would be caught, and a man who is awake and ready may not be. Julia was awake and struck a light, which suggests that being ready is what separates the two.

reads: a long thin cane
text: Two weapons, for two threats: the pistol is for a man, and the long thin cane is for something small that comes along the rope. The matches and candle-stump are what Julia reached for. When it comes, Holmes will strike a light and strike at the rope.

reads: a long drawn catlike whine
text: The cheetah is at the very window, but the shutters are barred and can't be worked from outside. The loose beasts are atmosphere, not the means.

reads: Twelve struck, and one and two and three, and still we sat waiting silently for whatever might befall.
text: Three has struck and nothing has happened. My prediction of an attempt 'at about three' needs loosening, so the whistle is probably not a clock.

reads: a strong smell of burning oil and heated metal
text: After three, a flash of light appears at the ventilator and goes out at once. Then comes a smell of burning oil and hot metal, and Watson hears quiet movement next door.

reads: Someone in the next room had lit a dark-lantern
text: A lantern lit next door shows through the ventilator, so the vent opens into Roylott's room. He is awake and at work in the small hours, as he was on the night Julia died.

A smell has crossed from his room to ours, as cigar smoke once did. Air passes freely through the opening and the wall is not sealed to it. The smell is the lantern's, so it does not point to any poison vapour.
The gleam is brief. He may have looked through to see whether the room is dark and the bed occupied. He sees nothing, so Holmes's darkness holds.

reads: like that of a small jet of steam escaping continually from a kettle
text: About half an hour later, a soft continuous hiss. Holmes springs up at once and lashes at the bell-pull.
A soft hiss like escaping steam is how a snake sounds. It would also suit a leaking gas pipe, but I already half-suspected a snake.
hindsight: A first-time reader needs to link the hiss to the earlier idea of a small Indian creature on the rope. The description fits steam or gas equally.

reads: lashed furiously with his cane at the bell-pull
text: Holmes strikes at the rope the instant he hears the sound. He knew what it meant and where it was. Gas or a poison on the cord cannot be beaten with a cane, so what is on the rope is a thing with a body. The vapour and poison options fall away.
The dummy rope is a road from the vent to the pillow, and the clamped bed keeps the sleeper at the end of it. Holmes is guarding exactly that road.

reads: You see it, Watson?
text: Holmes expects Watson to be able to see it by match-light. It is a visible object, and he has given up silence now that it has come.

reads: I heard a low, clear whistle
text: A second listener hears the whistle. Watson had been told of it, so he may be primed, but he was awake and the night was quiet, so the whistle is probably real. He does not say where it came from.

The whistle came as the match was struck, which fits Roylott seeing the light through the vent. On the fatal night the order was match, scream, whistle. It looks like his call to the thing once the plan is disturbed.

reads: He had ceased to strike and was gazing up at the ventilator
text: Holmes is pale with horror and loathing, which a rope or a device would not provoke. He stops striking and looks up at the vent. Something alive has gone back up the way it came.

reads: a hoarse yell of pain and fear and anger all mingled in the one dreadful shriek
text: Right after the thing is driven back, a terrible cry comes from the next room, and it includes pain. Roylott seems to have been hurt by something, probably what was sent down the rope.
options: The creature turned on its master
He was hurt some other way
He cried out only in rage at the failure

reads: They say that away down in the village
text: The cry carried to the village and the parsonage. Watson only has this by report. It would explain how the 'widespread rumours' about Roylott's death began.

reads: It means that it is all over
text: Holmes does not rush to help. He treats the cry as an end and as perhaps 'for the best'. Roylott is dead or dying, which is the death Watson advertised.
The preface said Roylott dies and the truth is terrible. Tonight he seems to die of his own scheme, which fits the option that the wrongdoer perishes by it.

reads: Twice he struck at the chamber door without any reply from within.
text: No answer, and the door opens at the handle. Roylott cannot speak. He is dead or insensible, and he was awake enough to be hurt moments ago.

reads: his eyes were fixed in a dreadful, rigid stare at the corner of the ceiling
text: Roylott sits dead or rigid on the plain wooden chair in dressing-gown and slippers. The lantern beam falls on the safe, whose door is ajar. The short stock with the long lash lies across his lap. His eyes are fixed on the corner of the ceiling.

reads: throwing a brilliant beam of light upon the iron safe, the door of which was ajar
text: The lantern is trained on the open safe, the safe with the milk saucer on top. Something was kept there and has come out. The beam watches the place it should go back to.

His seat is the plain wooden chair Holmes studied, and he is looking at the corner of the ceiling, presumably where the vent is. The chair serves the opening. Holmes has still not said what he saw on its seat.

reads: Across his lap lay the short stock with the long lash which we had noticed during the day
text: The looped lash has been taken from the bed to his lap. It was a tool he was using or about to use, which fits a noose for handling a dangerous creature.

reads: clad in a long grey dressing-gown
text: On the fatal night Helen met him in his dressing-gown, and tonight he sits up in one at his post. He was probably up and waiting then too, which explains why he came out so promptly once Helen called.

reads: Round his brow he had a peculiar yellow band, with brownish speckles
text: This must be Julia's 'speckled band', but is it cloth or living? A spotted headcloth would match Helen's gipsy guess, and Roylott is friendly with the gipsies. But why would a man wear one bound tight at night in his own room, and why does Watson say it only 'seemed' bound?
options: The creature itself, coiled on his head
hindsight: The second option is easy once the ending is known. At this point a reader needs the earlier snake guess, or the oddity of a tight headcloth, to prefer it.

reads: The band! the speckled band!
text: Holmes says Julia's words in a whisper. Nobody whispers about a cloth. He treats it as Julia's band and as something that must not be roused, so the band is probably the creature he just lashed at.

reads: there reared itself from among his hair the squat diamond-shaped head and puffed neck of a loathsome serpent
text: The 'speckled band' is a snake, coiled round his head so that it looked like a banded cloth. This answers the question of what Julia meant.
The headcloth reading goes, and with it Helen's gipsy handkerchiefs. The word 'band' was literal but not in the way she guessed.

This explains the sealed room, the missing marks and the missing poison. A snake passes through a vent no person could use, leaves only tiny punctures that a coroner could miss, and its venom is not one the doctors tested for. Roylott's Calcutta years and his Indian pets now look like preparation.

reads: the deadliest snake in India
text: Holmes names it a swamp adder, the deadliest snake in India. He says Roylott died within ten seconds of the bite.

Helen said Indian animals were 'sent over to him by a correspondent', and now an Indian snake is the weapon. It was kept in the safe, fed from the saucer, and run along the dummy rope. The creature hypothesis is confirmed.

reads: Violence does, in truth, recoil upon the violent
text: Roylott is both the schemer and the victim of his scheme. This settles the opening question about his death and shows what Watson meant by rumours worse than the truth.
The order was lash, retreat to the vent, then Roylott's cry. Driven back by Holmes's blows, the snake probably turned on its master, who was sitting watching the vent.
options: Driven back, it bit its master
It had already bitten him before it reached us

reads: He has died within ten seconds of being bitten.
text: Holmes did not time it. Julia lived long enough to unlock her door, speak, be given brandy and 'slowly sink'. That is minutes, or more, against his ten seconds. His figure is probably a flourish, and the difference between the two deaths is not explained.

reads: remove Miss Stoner to some place of shelter
text: Helen is alive and is to be sheltered. As guessed, she came through and can be the lady of Watson's pledge. The one who died is Roylott.

reads: threw it into the iron safe, which he closed upon it
text: Holmes loops the noose over the snake's neck, carries it at arm's length, throws it into the safe and shuts the door.

reads: throwing the noose round the reptile
text: The tied lash is a noose for handling the snake. This answers the oddity of a dog lash tied in a loop, in a house with no dog.

The safe is the snake's den, as the open door and the milk implied. An iron door shutting on it makes a clang like 'a mass of metal'. On the fatal night Roylott probably whistled the snake back and shut it in, which fits the order scream, whistle, clang.
The saucer of milk on the safe, in a house with no cat, was the snake's food, going by the popular tale. Holmes's talk of a cat was a hint at it.

Still open: how Roylott found Baker Street; what his 'important business' in town was; what Holmes saw on the chair; whether the money would have survived Helen's death; why Julia lingered when Roylott died 'within ten seconds'; and how Roylott trained a snake to the rope and the whistle.

Final picture: Roylott, who stood to lose a third of his income at each marriage, fitted a false ventilator and rope to Julia's room around her engagement. He kept a swamp adder in his safe, sent it down the rope by night and whistled it back. It killed Julia. He then moved Helen into that clamped bed through sham repairs. Holmes's lashing drove it back and it killed its master. The gipsies, the big animals, fright and ordinary poison all fall away. Helen survives.
options: Roylott acted alone with the snake, for Julia and Helen alike
An accomplice such as the correspondent or the gipsies helped
Julia's death had some other cause
